blocking_findings.violation: On macOS, installClient() always runs an independent codesign/Developer-ID signature check (verifyBundle) on the downloaded bundle regardless of whether a checksum was available. On Windows, installClientWindows() has no equivalent signature/Authenticode check at all — it trusts whatever spec.resolve() returns and only verifies a SHA-256 inside downloadToFile, and only `if (sha256 && ...)` is truthy. For Claude Desktop on Windows, that sha256 comes from `picked.InstallerSha256` in a community-maintained winget-pkgs YAML manifest, read via resolveClaudeDesktopWindows with no runtime check that the field is a non-empty string before it is trusted (the TS type says it's required, but parseYaml of a manifest missing/blank-ing that key at runtime yields undefined, which is falsy). If a manifest entry has no InstallerSha256, downloadToFile silently skips its own checksum comparison, and installClientWindows then runs the downloaded installer.exe with elevated silent args and zero verification of any kind.
blocking_findings.why_blocking: A missing or tampered checksum field in a third-party-maintained manifest (or a future ClientSpec added without a guaranteed-populated sha256) causes CodeMie to download and silently execute an unverified Windows installer under the user's account, with no fallback signature check the way the macOS path has. This is a supply-chain execution risk introduced by extending the trust model to a new OS without carrying over the second verification layer.
blocking_findings.remedy: In resolveClaudeDesktopWindows (and generally before returning any ClientDownload used by installClientWindows), throw if the resolved sha256 is missing/empty rather than letting downloadToFile's checksum check become a no-op; and/or add a Windows-side authenticity check (e.g. validate the installer's Authenticode publisher certificate) so the Windows path isn't solely dependent on a hash sourced from the same feed it is meant to validate.

blocking_findings.violation: code-quality.md requires comments to accurately describe current behavior ('comment the why, not the what'; JSDoc on public APIs). The file header JSDoc still describes a macOS-only installer ('for the current macOS user', 'Apps go into ~/Applications') and the macOS-specific checksum/signature policy, without updating it to describe the Windows path this change adds or its different (checksum-only) trust model.
blocking_findings.why_blocking: The header is the documented contract a maintainer reads first; it is now inaccurate about which platforms are supported and what security guarantee applies on each, which caused this change to omit the trust-model asymmetry noted above.
blocking_findings.remedy: Update the file header to mention Windows, where apps install into Program Files / LocalAppData, and to call out explicitly that Windows installers are checksum-verified only (no signature check), rather than leaving the comment macOS-only.
